note: A's proposal is synthesized once per scenario and reused across its three conditions, so the clips differ only in B's vocalization

clips.relationship: Speaker A and Speaker B are co-directors of a volunteer theater troupe.
clips.shared_context: Their rented auditorium unexpectedly closed for repairs three weeks before opening night. Canceling would mean refunding ticket sales and losing much of the troupe's modest budget. The group has staged indoor productions for years, but the city park's covered bandstand is available for summer events and has never been used by the troupe. Moving there would avoid the auditorium cost, but it would require adapting the set, lighting, and rehearsals on short notice.
clips.proposal: What if we turn the show into a one-weekend outdoor production at the park bandstand?
clips.gold_inferred_state: B appears to think an outdoor bandstand production is too far-fetched to be a serious solution.
clips.gold_response_function: Establish that the proposal is serious and defend its practical feasibility.
clips.gold_response: I'm serious—the parks office can fast-track the permit, and we would avoid paying for another venue.

clips.relationship: Speaker A is the finance manager and Speaker B is the development director at a small local museum.
clips.shared_context: The museum's annual gala is six weeks away and usually funds a large part of its operating budget. This year, ticket sales are lagging, while an urgent roof repair has become more expensive than expected. Speaker B and a small staff have spent months arranging the venue, auction items, and donor invitations, and the museum has never canceled its gala before. The venue contract still allows cancellation, though the museum would lose its deposit.
clips.proposal: What if we cancel this year's gala and put the remaining event budget straight into the roof repair?
clips.gold_inferred_state: B appears to think canceling the gala is so unrealistic that A may not seriously believe it is financially viable.
clips.gold_response_function: Establish that the proposal is serious and defend its financial logic.
clips.gold_response: I'm serious—the deposit is smaller than what we'd lose trying to stage a gala that isn't selling.

clips.relationship: Speaker A is the owner of an independent bookstore, and Speaker B is the longtime store manager.
clips.shared_context: The bookstore has occupied the same neighborhood storefront for nearly twenty years and is known for its reading room and weekly author events. Sales have increasingly shifted to online orders, and the landlord has offered a new lease with a steep rent increase. The shop can cover its current bills, but the new rent would leave little room for staff or events. A nearby café has offered to host occasional book pop-ups, but neither A nor B has previously discussed giving up the storefront.
clips.proposal: What if we don’t renew the lease and run the shop online with weekend pop-ups instead?
clips.gold_inferred_state: B appears to think abandoning the storefront for pop-ups is so contrary to the bookstore's identity that A may not be serious.
clips.gold_response_function: Establish that the proposal is serious and explain the financial reason it is worth considering.
clips.gold_response: I am serious—the new lease would swallow almost everything we make on the store floor.
